q: How many Avari stayed behind at Cuiviénen?
a: The Nature of Middle-earth DOES count them, repeatedly and with different results — 5,000 remaining against 10,000 marching in one scheme; 8,748 Avari against 17,496 Eldar in another; 16,056 and 9,000 elsewhere. What is missing is not a number but a settled one, and any count of the Avari in later Ages.
r: The demographic model carries them as a stated blank; no eastern census exists. — Corrected 2026-07-24: the earlier entry claimed the corpus 'never counts them'. It counts them several times over, in figures Tolkien did not reconcile.

q: What are the populations of Harad, Rhûn and Khand?
a: Armies beyond counting are attested — at the Morannon, LotR V.10, 'forces ten times and more than ten times their match would ring them in a sea of enemies', against the seven thousands the lords could lead out — but never a census, a city-count, or a homeland survey. — LotR V.9-10; App A II; UT for the Easterlings
r: The armies model derives lower bounds from hosts and refuses totals.

q: How do Orcs reproduce — and are there female Orcs?
a: HoME X says they 'had life and multiplied after the manner of the Children of Ilúvatar', and Myths Transformed in the same volume says a good deal more. They 'bred and multiplied rapidly whenever left undisturbed'; they 'needed food and drink, and rest'; and their lifespan is stated outright — 'they died and were not immortal, even according to the manner of the Quendi; indeed they appear to have been by nature short-lived compared with the span of Men of higher race, such as the Edain'. One mode of breeding is named too, of Men reduced to the Orc-level: 'they would or could be made to mate with Orcs, producing new breeds, often larger and more cunning'. What is genuinely undescribed is a female Orc — no she-orc, orc-woman or orc-mother appears as whole words anywhere in Tolkien's own texts — the tier-1 and tier-2 shelf, which is the only place a silence about what he wrote can be established. FOUR TIER-3 WORKS DO USE THE TERMS, and every one of them agrees the description is absent rather than supplying it: Picturing Tolkien, which states that neither Tolkien nor Jackson portrays Orc women, The Complete Guide ('Nothing is said about Orkish tribal structures or female Orcs'), Shippey, who asks why readers never encounter them, and Mallorn 54, which canvasses a speculative parthenogenesis reading. They are second readers agreeing with us, not witnesses to the legendarium.
r: Orc numbers in the archive are army-derived only, with the gap flagged on every chart. — Corrected 2026-07-28: the entry had declared family and lifespan nowhere described. Both are described in Myths Transformed — the same volume, HoME X, that the entry cites for its own quotation. Only the female Orc is a real silence, and it is kept.

q: How large were the hosts of the War of Wrath?
a: The corpus gives outcomes — Thangorodrim broken, Beleriand drowned, the dragon-fleet's last sortie — but not one number for either side. Silm 24 arrays the host of the Valar by kindred, 'the Vanyar, the people of Ingwë, and those also of the Noldor who never departed from Valinor', and counts none of them. — Silm 24
r: The battle stands in the armies hall as a dashed, unnumbered marker with the exact refusal.

q: What strength assailed Lórien and Mirkwood in 3019?
a: App B records three assaults on Lórien and the long battle under the trees — outcomes only, no figures.
r: Two dashed markers in the armies hall carry the refusal verbatim.

a: Three cited exceptions exist — the nissi in desperate defence, Haleth's guard, Éowyn — and no counts for any of them. — HoME X, Laws & Customs; UT, The Drúedain; LotR V.6
r: The armies model reports female share ≈ 0 with exceptions named, rather than inventing percentages.

a: The last son of Fëanor cast his Silmaril into the sea; the Silmarillion leaves him wandering the shores in lament — and never ends his story.
r: His genealogy card reads 'unknown (wanders)' — the archive's only open-ended Fëanorian.

a: Tolkien answered this twice, and differently. In Letter 144, to Naomi Mitchison: they 'had disappeared for good, being destroyed with their gardens in the War of the Last Alliance… when Sauron pursued a scorched earth policy and burned their land'. In Letter 338 he withdraws it: 'As for the Entwives: I do not know.' The narrative itself keeps only the lost gardens and Treebeard's grief.
r: The Ents' population line runs to extinction with fertility zero — and the question stays a question. — Corrected 2026-07-24: the archive previously showed only the narrative silence and neither of Tolkien's own answers. Sources: Letters 144 and 338.

a: Within the tale he is deliberately unexplained — Tolkien confirms the opacity is intentional. Outside it he does gloss him, in Letter 153 to Peter Hastings: Bombadil is 'an “allegory”, or an exemplar, a particular embodying of pure (real) natural science: the spirit that desires knowledge of other things, their history and nature, because they are “other” and wholly independent of the enquiring mind'.
r: He appears nowhere in the archive's trees, peoples or armies — deliberately. — Corrected 2026-07-24: what the corpus withholds is a taxonomy, not an account. Letter 153 gives the account. Source: Letter 153 (draft).

a: After Sam's blade and the Phial, the text says only that this tale does not record it. — LotR IV.10
r: Her lair is pinned on the map; her end is not.

q: What was the mithril-coat's final road?
a: last attested worn at the Scouring of the Shire, 3 Nov 3019 — and then the corpus falls silent; over Sea or left behind, no text says. — LotR VI.8; App B
r: The artifact chain ends with the gap declared, not bridged.

a: The corpus never names her, and that clause is exact: across tiers 1 and 2 the only entry for her is an index line, "'Tradition of Isildur'; Isildur's wife." What it does record of her is not what this entry used to say. She did sail — when Sauron took Minas Ithil in S.A. 3429, Isildur 'went with his wife and his sons by ship down the River, and they sailed from the mouths of Anduin seeking Elendil', which the Tale of Years reads as 'sails north from Anduin's Mouths to Elendil in Arnor, with his wife and sons'. But the youngest son was not aboard: 'Valandil son of Isildur' was 'born in Imladris' the year after, in 3430. And the corpus leaves her in the north-east, not the south — 'his wife and his youngest son, Valandil, he had left in Imladris when he went to the war', and Isildur was riding to Imladris, 'for he had left his wife and youngest son there', when he was killed at the Gladden Fields. The southward sailing belongs to a different pair: in the Akallabêth 'Isildur and Anárion were borne away southwards' out of the Downfall — two brothers, and no wife in the sentence.
r: The family trees carry the marriage as an unnamed node would lie — they simply do not draw what is not given. — Corrected 2026-07-28: the entry had given her a voyage south from the wreck of the realm with the youngest son. She did sail, but from Minas Ithil in S.A. 3429 with Isildur and their sons, and the Tale of Years takes them north to Arnor; the youngest son, Valandil, was born in Imladris the year after; and it is at Imladris that the corpus leaves her. Only the namelessness was right, and it stands.

a: App A counts five children of Thengel and names two; three daughters go unnamed forever.
r: The genealogy notes the count and draws only the named.

a: She is named once, and the name belongs to Felagund — not to Orodreth. In The War of the Jewels an addition to QS §137, made “after the words 'he [Felagund] gave to Barahir his ring'”, reads that he 'sent away his wife Meril to her own folk in Eglorest, and with her went their son, yet an elvenchild, and Gilgalad Starlight he was called'. Christopher Tolkien glosses it on the next line — 'Felagund's wife Meril has not been named before, nor any child of his' — and the volume's index agrees: 'Meril  Wife of Felagund.' In the Orodreth variant, on the same page, she is NOT named: that note, struck out, reads only 'he commanded Orodreth to send away his son Gilgalad, and wife', and of a third note CT writes 'A blank space is here left for the name of Felagund's wife.' The late Peoples of Middle-earth text, which does make Gil-galad the son of Orodreth, likewise leaves her unnamed: 'Their mother was a Sindarin lady of the North. She called her son Gil-galad.' Under the published descent from Fingon, no mother is named at all.
r: The trees show all three paternal variants; the maternal line is a blank the archive refuses to fill. — Corrected 2026-07-24: the archive previously asserted that no version ever names a mother. One does. — Corrected 2026-07-28: that correction found the right passage and gave it the wrong father. Meril is Felagund's wife, in a variant where Gil-galad is Felagund's son; in the Orodreth variant she is not named, which is what this entry had denied. Source: HoME XI p. 242 and its index.

a: A grandmother 'stern and wise' rules the clan by the Gladden; between her and him, no parent is named. Déagol's kinship is NOT unspecified: Letter 214 (to A. C. Nunn, a draft) calls him 'evidently a relative (as no doubt all the members of the small community were)' — Tolkien's own inference, so the fact of kinship is given and only its degree is not.
r: The parentage stands as an honest dashed link in the trees; the Sméagol–Déagol link is kin of unnamed degree, not 'friend' alone.

q: How did Narsil come from Telchar's forge to Elendil's hand?
a: First Age Nogrod to Second Age Númenor — an heirloom road of thousands of years with not one recorded holder between. — Silm 22; App A I(iii)
r: The artifact chain marks it 'honest gap' in so many words.

a: The corpus places it, though it cannot be reached: 'far off in the east of Middle-earth, and northward, and it was a bay in the Inland Sea of Helcar'. The Ambarkanta sets it 'to the North beside the waters of Helkar' and Christopher notes it is shown on map IV. NoME even measures it — 2,000 miles as the crow flies from the coast of ancient Beleriand.
r: The living map ends where the corpus's geography ends; Cuiviénen is cited, not pinned. — Corrected 2026-07-24: the location is given in the same sentence the archive had quoted to prove it unknown. What is truly lost is the land itself, drowned in the changing of the world.

q: What lies in the far East and South?
a: Client-kingdoms, rumour, and one real account. No map, no census, no city-count and no homeland survey — but not nothing, and Khand is the proof. The corpus gives it a location, 'Khand  Land south-east of Mordor'; a people, 'Variags  The people of Khand'; a diplomacy — the Wainriders 'were in conflict with the peoples of Khand and their neighbours further south. Eventually a peace and alliance was agreed between these enemies of Gondor'; a dated war, the assault of 1944, in which they 'made alliance with men of Khand and of Near Harad; and in this great assault from north and south, Gondor came near to destruction'; and a place on the field, 'Easterlings with axes, and Variags of Khand'. Nor is the East wholly unrecorded: PoME says of the two Blue Wizards, there named Morinehtar and Rómestámo, that they 'must have had very great influence on the history of the Second Age and Third Age in weakening and disarraying the forces of East'. Tolkien's note reads 'the forces of East', without the article, and is quoted here as it stands. What is missing is a narrative and a set of numbers, not every trace.
r: The realm-slices mark Rhûn 'schematic'; nothing further is drawn. — Corrected 2026-07-24: the entry previously claimed no history of the East exists. — Corrected 2026-07-28: the Blue Wizards quotation had gained a definite article — 'the forces of the East' for 'the forces of East' — so the archive's own matcher could no longer find the archive's own quote. Restored to the wording of the note printed in PoME (HoME XII). — Corrected 2026-07-28: and the same sentence still carried 'nothing at all of Khand', eight words before the clause the 2026-07-24 sweep came to fix. Khand is named as whole words in five tier-1 volumes and has a location, a people, a diplomatic history, a dated war and a battlefield appearance. What it has no figure for is population.

q: What did Númenor look like, city by city?
a: UT gives one map-description chapter and a handful of places; the island drowned with its geography mostly unwritten.
r: The archive renders Númenor as data (population, fleets, kings) — not as a mapped land.
